title: The First New Album in Two Decades
summary: Kerrie Bolton, Andrew Withycombe and Bart Cummings discuss reuniting to make A Place In My Memory Is All I Have To Claim, their first Hydroplane album in twenty years.
transcript:
Kerrie Bolton, Andrew Withycombe and Bart Cummings of Hydroplane joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios to talk about A Place In My Memory Is All I Have To Claim, their first album in more than two decades. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 6 November 2025. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Hydroplane was, of course, one of the names Dean Wareham from Galaxie 500 considered before settling on Luna for his project. It being available, Hydroplane sort of flew in and adopted it as their own. Hydroplane have staked such an important place in the local music community and internationally, and we should welcome three members of the group: Kerrie Bolton, Andrew Withycombe and Bart Cummings.

Simon: By way of brief introduction, you formed in the mid-1990s, as Lauren mentioned. There were three albums between 1997 and 2001, before you stepped away as a collective for almost a quarter of a century, so we were thrilled to receive news from Efficient Space that there was to be a new album: A Place In My Memory Is All I Have To Claim.

There are, of course, historical connections with the Cat's Miaow, a group you were all involved with. And Hydroplane established a unique sonic identity by replacing live drums with loops and samples: famously, a Roland Jupiter-4 synthesiser and a sampler with two seconds of memory, with which you produced all manner of fascinating extended pieces.

There were lots of international connections. John Peel played you over 20 times, and there were international labels too. But almost 25 years have passed since that period, and we're so keen to hear what's been happening in the meantime.

Lauren: It is an especially long hiatus. We worked out that it's almost as long as the gap between the second and third seasons of Twin Peaks. When you were writing new music, did you feel obliged to your past selves, or was there a real freedom to redefine the band?

Andrew: I tend to think that the only band we're ever going to get compared to is our younger selves. That said, though, you've just got to go through and not worry about what people are going to think or say. But, yeah, we're aware of our history, but we're not slaves to it.

Simon: It sounds like a perfect balance, then: an observance of your origins, but also a freedom to embrace your own creative impulses. We've been very lucky because Efficient Space reissued some of your early material in 2022 and 2023, which really brought the music back into circulation. Did those releases play a role in deciding to get back together, or was the timing coincidental?

Bart: Yeah, definitely. There was, I guess, a little bit more time in our lives, but certainly the interest allowed us to get more interested in doing — I mean, it snowballed.

Kerrie: I didn't think we'd be doing this much.

Andrew: But it allowed us just to get back together and do things. There'd been a vibe for years anyway, and various offers, but with Efficient Space, we liked Michael, and it just felt right. So that's why we did the reissue, and plus there were Cat's Miaow things happening as well.

Bart: We'd spent probably the best part of 18 months just in communication for the reissues: 'Oh, someone's asked us to do this.' 'What do you think of this artwork?' Things like that.

And just from being in fairly regular contact with each other about the reissues, it was like, 'What are you doing in a month's time? Do you want to just get together and play some new music?' We had got together just before any of the reissues happened, so it wasn't a case of, 'Oh, they've become popular, let's follow up on that.' We got together, and it still felt good.

Kerrie: I guess the benefit, in our situation, is that we never really broke up. We never fell out. There wasn't anything to resolve, or any hurdles in that sense.

Andrew: So when we did get back together, it was on the quiet, just in case, 'Oh, whatever we had is well and truly gone.' But it's just the enjoyment of making music with these people that is why we're doing it. That we got an album out of it that is, I think, as good as anything we've done in the past is a bonus.

Lauren: You mentioned Michael Kucyk from Efficient Space, who's played a pretty significant role in the band's recent chapters. How did you first connect with Michael?

Bart: He just contacted us. It took him a while; I think my spam filter was sort of… He knows lots of people we know, and eventually he got in touch, which was quite surprising.

Lauren: He described your new album landing in his inbox as a complete surprise. Does that mean you didn't even tell him you were working on these new songs?

Andrew: Well, we hinted, but I wanted to make sure that he liked what we were doing. He'd always said he would do anything we did, so we wanted a complete album, but I wanted to make sure he liked it. So we completely finished it first.

Kerrie: Yeah, because I think he was surprised we had finished it. It was a great reaction.

Simon: The title of the new record, A Place In My Memory Is All I Have To Claim, is a really evocative one. We heard it was prompted by something, Andrew, that you found while searching through newspaper archives. What drew you to that phrase?

Andrew: Yeah, it was in the National Library's Trove newspaper database, and I did see something similar in a poem, like a hundred-year-old poem. But I stupidly didn't take a copy, and I just kind of twisted it to the way I thought it should be. I like to read old newspapers. They're quite inspiring sometimes.

Lauren: I was listening to an interview you did recently on 4ZZZ, where you mentioned you spend a bit of time searching through Trove in particular. Is that casual browsing, or more serious research?

Andrew: Casual, and serious for work sometimes, yes.

Lauren: And are you looking for specific things, or gliding through the archives for inspiration?

Andrew: Look, it varies. Sometimes it's inspiration: you'll just search a phrase or something. But other times, it's more a particular thing.

Simon: Reading through the track list and listening to the album, there's so much that's evocative, and when we talk about historical archives, there's a song on the new album called 'Incident at Westall'. It refers to a famous 1966 UFO sighting here in Victoria, in which about 200 students and teachers witnessed unidentified flying objects circling their heads and landing in nearby fields in broad daylight. According to Australian Geographic, it's a mystery that's unsolved to this day. What aspect of that story most interests you, and how did it find a place on the album?

Andrew: Because I'm sort of the Geezer Butler of the band, I wrote most of the lyrics. I'd read an article in Good Weekend where some people, who must have been in their late 60s or 70s, were reflecting on that, and how they thought there was a girl who went crazy and never came back, things like that.

Until I'd read that, I'd never heard of it, and I just thought it was a really interesting story. Thinking about how we remember these things: I'd never heard of it, but obviously they had been there. How does their memory of it fit with what happened? It's just a cool story.

Lauren: The album is filled with interesting stories, and beautiful and engaging themes. Maybe, Kerrie, we could talk to you about your relationship with some of the ideas explored on the album. The press material lists human cruelty, flight, adventure, space travel. On a personal level, how are you connecting with these ideas, and do you see a thread running through the record?

Kerrie: Sort of. When they give me the songs to learn, I try and make it personal, and I do my research too, and ask what they're about.

Andrew: Not really. It's memory, but I think things like 'The Loneliest Astronaut' are really an allegory of human cruelty, of what's going on now. Without getting too political, because I don't want to offend people, I was definitely thinking of things that are happening, whether it's Sudan or Gaza. Even though the song is about animals in space, it's more than that. And then there are some songs that are definitely about us, and others that are just about the recent past.

Simon: Let's talk about the sound of the record. You've talked about creating all the sounds on the album yourselves. Can you tell us more about this process, and the unspecified electronic devices you're using?

Bart: Andrew likes rules, and one of the rules for this one was that we were only going to sample ourselves. So there are lots of things that are looped, et cetera, but they're just noises and pieces of music that we've created internally.

When I'm at home mucking around and making a noise, I tend to go, 'This sounds cool, I'll just film it on my phone,' and I'll whack that up as an Instagram story. Then invariably, a few weeks later, Andrew will send me a song with something sampled from what I've uploaded on Instagram.

Andrew: In a lot of ways, we've just been relatively low tech. We don't MIDI. Well, we loop things. It's very much people playing sounds, apart from when that's looped. And it kind of has a retrofuturist feel to it. We're quite into a lot of 50s and 60s electronica, where you hear it and then you go, 'Oh, God, that's just a loop of tape going around, and then modifying it.' There's not a lot of electronics as such. So that aspect, the way we work, has been maintained from a lot of our releases.

Simon: Kerrie, your voice is such a striking centrepiece of the sound of Hydroplane, and the Cat's Miaow as well. We were fascinated and thrilled to learn about your parallel career as an opera singer, performing with Opera Australia and teaching voice. How is it to switch between operatic technique and the singing style of Hydroplane?

Kerrie: Well, they're the antithesis of each other. Singing operatically is a very physical and very focused sound, whereas with this I can just be really delicate and light. And I can call it musing sometimes, if you're not really singing with a full voice. It's quite a relief and a pleasure to be able to do that. Singing operatically can be quite exhausting.

Simon: It's a particularly demanding skill on a technical level. Do you find a liberation in the singing approach of Hydroplane?

Kerrie: Yeah, absolutely. And I've learnt to love reverb. It's one of my favourite things. Hearing the effects the guys put on really simple singing is just really lovely. I enjoy it.

Lauren: In the early days, the band received mixed reviews. Did you feel that what you were doing was sometimes misunderstood back in the 90s?

Kerrie: No comment.

Bart: I don't really think about it, to be perfectly honest. We just did our thing.

Andrew: I don't know that it was misunderstood, even. For the most part, it just seemed like it went out into a vacuum, and we didn't hear anything back, good, bad or indifferent. I remember we got a phone call saying, 'Oh, John Peel's playing it.' And we were just like, 'Oh, that's cool.' And that was as far as it went. But the weirdest thing is that now we're doing things like this, and people are noticing us, and people are receptive to what we're doing.

Bart's got this ongoing thing with emails headed 'Things that didn't happen in the 90s', and this would fall into it. 'We're being asked to come into RRR. Okay, yeah.' Venues contacting us, promoters contacting us: things like that just never happened.

Kerrie: Yeah, it's great. It's very gratifying.

Andrew: I kind of look back at the 90s, and we were a bit out of time, a bit out of place. But we were never really chasing —

Lauren: Maybe you were ahead of your time.

Andrew: It was just about recording, really. We'd focus on writing and recording, and that was enough. We didn't play live that much. We just felt the best use of our time and energy was in documenting what we were doing. Ridiculously, it has paid off 30 years down the track, in that we had a back catalogue ready to be rolled out when there was an audience for it.

Simon: It's beautiful to hear that there's a growing list of things that didn't happen in the 90s that you're able to enjoy and celebrate now, and to see you getting the chance to enjoy the almost mythological status the band has cultivated. You mentioned that you were never much of a live band, more a studio-based project, but in February this year you played at the NTS Naarm event. How did it feel to be back in the live incarnation? Is it maybe the start of a new chapter of live performances?

Kerrie: It's kind of lovely, really, because we have fun recording, but it can be quite separate. It's not in the same room at the same time. So actually playing — we didn't miss out back in the 90s, because these guys were playing in other bands and I was pursuing the opera thing. So we were all performing, but it's really lovely to be able to do this, and do it together. It's really nice.

Bart: Playing live, for me, there are two parts. We'll physically all be in the same room to do a rehearsal, which doesn't happen otherwise, and that's always fun. And without fail, there'll be someone in the audience who's in tears, because they thought they'd never get to see us play live. Something like that is quite grounding.

Kerrie: It's like they've just seen a unicorn.

Bart: That is very gratifying. And it's really nice to be able to give it to people.

Lauren: Congratulations on the new record, 24 years in the making. So great to finally have it here.
